rationale: I'm adding the aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each channel in each condition. It is the slope of the log-PSD against log-frequency, fitted on 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz so the alpha peak and line noise are left out. In ADHD it is thought to track the cortical excitation/inhibition balance, and it is separate from the oscillatory band ratios. A slope is unaffected by amplitude scale, so it should hold up on the external datasets. I've left the offset (intercept) out because it depends on amplitude scale.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few contaminated 2-s windows (eye blinks and movement in the low frequencies, muscle bursts in beta/gamma) can dominate a mean-averaged Welch spectrum. That inflates delta and gamma, distorts the relative theta/beta profile, and biases it differently depending on recording length and site. This round switches to a median across Welch segments, a robust spectral estimate that discards transient artifacts without explicit epoch rejection. The relative-band-power features, logistic regression and C=0.1 are unchanged, so any change in score comes from the spectral estimate alone.

I'm re-referencing every recording to the common average (subtracting the instantaneous mean across all 26 channels) before the Welch PSD. The original reference is in every channel, so it spreads one site's activity across the whole scalp and blurs the spatial pattern of the theta/beta profile. It also makes the features depend on the amplifier set-up, which matters because the external datasets use other references. The features, logistic regression and C=0.1 are unchanged, so any change in score comes from the re-referencing alone.

I'm splitting the coarse bands into physiologically distinct sub-bands: theta 4–6 and 6–8 Hz, alpha1 8–10 and alpha2 10–13 Hz, beta1 13–20 and beta2 20–30 Hz. Delta and gamma stay as they are. ADHD effects are reported mainly as slowed alpha (power moving from upper to lower alpha), excess low theta and reduced beta1, and 5 wide bands average these effects away. Everything else is unchanged (mean Welch spectrum, original reference, log relative power, L2 logistic regression with C=0.1), so any change in score comes from the band split alone.

Splitting the bands into sub-bands gave the largest gain so far (+0.03), so the detailed shape of the spectrum carries signal. This round goes further and uses 2-Hz bins of log relative power across 2–30 Hz, keeping one bin each for 1–2 Hz delta and 30–45 Hz gamma. That lets the model follow subject-level shifts such as alpha slowing, low-theta excess and the beta1 dip without fixed band edges blurring them. Everything else is unchanged (mean Welch spectrum, original reference, L2 logistic regression with C=0.1), so any change in score comes from the finer binning alone.

The fine-bin model has 832 strongly correlated log-relative-power features and only a few hundred subjects. Regularization strength is now the main bias/variance control, and C=0.1 was fixed rather than chosen. This round picks C from a log grid using grouped inner 5-fold CV on the training fold only (`ctx["groups_train"]`, scored by AUROC). Features and model are otherwise unchanged, so any change in score comes from data-driven shrinkage alone.

Keep the same 2-Hz log relative power bins, but represent eyes-open as its change from eyes-closed (EO − EC, the reactivity) rather than as raw EO values. Reduced alpha blocking and altered arousal reactivity are reported in ADHD. Raw EC and EO bins are highly correlated, so after standardization the L2 penalty barely uses their small difference. Giving the difference its own standardized features should let the classifier weight that within-subject signal properly; the difference is also free of per-subject offsets. The feature span, classifier and C=0.1 are unchanged, so any change in score comes from this reparametrization alone.

Last time, switching from the mean to the median Welch spectrum cost −0.05. That suggests transient, non-stationary activity carries ADHD signal, such as vigilance fluctuations, drowsiness bursts and movement or blink episodes, and averaging it out discards it. This round adds per-channel temporal variability: the standard deviation over 2-s windows of log band power in five coarse bands, for each condition. This measures EEG-vigilance instability, and it is unaffected by amplitude scale and recording length. The existing fine-bin relative power features and the classifier are unchanged.

I'm adding long-range temporal correlations: a DFA exponent of the amplitude envelope in the theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) bands, per channel and condition, fitted over 1–20 s. Last round's variability features gained +0.008, which suggests ADHD shows up in how oscillations evolve over time and not only in their average spectrum. LRTC (Linkenkaer-Hansen-style DFA) has been reported as reduced in ADHD, and the exponent does not depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length.

The DFA exponents of the theta, alpha and beta envelopes gave the biggest gain so far (+0.05), so how activity persists over time carries ADHD signal. This round extends the same DFA fit to the delta (1–4 Hz) and gamma (30–45 Hz) envelopes. Persistent delta can reflect drowsiness or slow-wave intrusions linked to low vigilance in ADHD, and persistent gamma/EMG can reflect motor restlessness. The exponent does not depend on amplitude scale or reference. Everything else is unchanged, so any change in score comes from the two extra bands alone.

This round replaces the single theta, alpha and beta DFA envelopes with physiological sub-bands: theta 4–6/6–8, alpha 8–10/10–13 and beta 13–20/20–30 Hz. Delta and gamma stay as they are. Splitting power into sub-bands gave the largest early gain, and ADHD effects are reported as specific to low vs high alpha and to beta1, so the wide bands may be averaging away separate long-range-correlation signals. The exponents still do not depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length, and everything else is unchanged.

Splitting bands into physiological sub-bands helped twice: once for power (round 4) and once for the DFA envelopes (+0.014 in round 11). The 2-s log-power variability features still use five coarse bands, so this round switches them to the same sub-bands: delta, theta 4–6/6–8, alpha 8–10/10–13, beta 13–20/20–30 and gamma. Vigilance-related fluctuations are expected to differ between low and high alpha and between low and high theta, and coarse bands would blur that. Everything else is unchanged.

The temporal-dynamics features gave the biggest gains so far: 2-s power variability added +0.008 and the DFA exponents added +0.05. Both look at slow timescales of 2 s or more. This round adds the fast, sub-second side: the coefficient of variation (std/mean) of the Hilbert amplitude envelope in each sub-band, per channel and condition. It measures how bursty the oscillations are, as opposed to sustained, which may differ in ADHD (unstable alpha/beta bursts, theta intrusions). The value does not depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length, and it reuses the envelopes already computed for DFA.

The temporal-dynamics features so far (variability, DFA and burstiness) describe each channel separately. This round adds how amplitude dynamics are coordinated across the scalp: for each channel, sub-band and condition, the mean Fisher-z correlation of its log amplitude envelope (downsampled to 25 Hz) with every other channel. That gives a per-channel amplitude-envelope-connectivity strength, which captures altered large-scale co-fluctuation in ADHD. It does not depend on amplitude scale or recording length, and it reuses the envelopes already computed for DFA.

I'm adding the oscillation-burst lifetime: the log mean duration (in seconds) of episodes where each sub-band's Hilbert envelope stays above its own 75th percentile, per channel and condition. The temporal-dynamics features have given the biggest gains (variability, DFA, envelope CV), but none of them directly measures how long bursts last, which Poil/Linkenkaer-Hansen-style lifetime analyses link to altered oscillation stability. The threshold is a per-channel percentile, so the value doesn't depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length, and it reuses envelopes the code already computes.

Burst lifetime gave +0.004 by measuring only the mean duration of supra-75th-percentile envelope episodes. Poil and Linkenkaer-Hansen showed that the useful signal sits in the heavy tail of the lifetime distribution: a few very long, sustained bursts produced by critical-like network dynamics. So this round adds the log 90th-percentile burst duration per channel, sub-band and condition. It reuses the same envelopes and per-channel threshold, so it stays independent of amplitude scale, reference and recording length.

I'm adding a new kind of temporal-dynamics feature: how stable the frequency of each sub-band oscillation is over time. For each sub-band, channel and condition, it is the log standard deviation of the Hilbert instantaneous frequency, averaged over 0.2-s blocks, and reuses the analytic signals the code already computes. The features kept so far measure amplitude dynamics (variability, DFA, envelope CV, burst lifetime). Unstable or wandering rhythms, such as alpha frequency jitter and theta/alpha switching under fluctuating vigilance, are a separate ADHD-relevant dynamic, and phase-based frequency does not depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length.

Frequency instability at 0.2 s gave a big gain (+0.023), and the slow-timescale amplitude features (2-s variability, DFA) each helped beyond their fast counterparts. So this round adds the slow side of frequency dynamics. For each sub-band, channel and condition it computes the log standard deviation of the Hilbert instantaneous frequency averaged over 2-s blocks. This captures slow, vigilance-related frequency drift (such as alpha slowing during drowsiness episodes) rather than fast jitter. It reuses the analytic signals already computed and does not depend on amplitude scale or reference.

This round adds amplitude–frequency coupling for each sub-band, channel and condition. It is the Pearson correlation, across 0.2-s blocks, between the block-mean log Hilbert envelope and the block-mean instantaneous frequency, reusing the analytic signals the code already computes. Envelope dynamics and frequency instability each helped on their own, but nothing yet links the two. Fluctuating vigilance in ADHD should couple them: alpha slows when it weakens in drowsy episodes, and theta/alpha switching comes with amplitude changes. A correlation does not depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length.

This adds cross-frequency phase–amplitude coupling. For each channel and condition it measures the normalized mean-vector-length modulation index between the phase of the slow sub-bands (delta, theta 4–6/6–8, alpha 8–10 Hz) and the amplitude envelope of the fast ones (beta 20–30, gamma 30–45 Hz), reusing the analytic signals already computed. Every feature kept so far describes a single frequency band. Theta–gamma and alpha–beta coupling, which coordinate fast local activity with slower rhythms, are reported as altered in ADHD. The index is divided by the mean amplitude, so it does not depend on amplitude scale, reference gain or recording length.
